\section{Experiments}

\subsection{Setup}

We evaluate on synthetic and semi-synthetic data generating processes (DGPs); full specifications appear in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
The synthetic DGP generates $N{=}5{,}000$ observations from a randomized trial with $K \in \{2, 4\}$ subgroups, controlled CATE heterogeneity $\Delta\tau$, and subgroup-specific symmetric misclassification rates with heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$.
Expert labels ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{50, \ldots, 2000\}$) are a simple random sample with true $Z$ observed; each configuration is repeated for 100 Monte Carlo runs.
The semi-synthetic DGP samples $N{=}5{,}000$ tweets from TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, defining $K{=}4$ subgroups by crossing hashtag presence and text length (unbalanced: 39\%/38\%/12\%/11\%), with misclassification rates $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$ reflecting empirical evidence that text features degrade LLM accuracy~\cite{ashwin2025bias}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup MLE without pooling), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Our Global baseline is equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} applied with a pooled (homogeneous) error rate; Stratified MLE corresponds to per-subgroup DSL without hierarchical shrinkage.
EC-HTE extends this by borrowing strength across subgroups via hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
Real-data validation on hate speech detection confirms $\Delta\pi = 0.117$ across text-feature subgroups (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Measurement error and annotation models.}
Classical measurement error theory shows that correction via estimated error models can amplify MSE when the error structure is misspecified~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}; Bayesian approaches require informative priors when identification is weak~\cite{gustafson2003measurement}, and nonparametric methods use repeated measurements or instruments to recover the true distribution~\cite{hu2008nonparametric}.
We formalize this principle for a specific causal estimand: Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} gives an exact identity for CATE bias under global correction with heterogeneous misclassification.
\citet{ogburn2012nondifferential} show nondifferential confounder misclassification attenuates effects; our setting differs---the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier, and correction can amplify bias.
\citet{battistin2014treatment} study treatment effect estimation with covariate measurement error but focus on average effects rather than subgroup-level heterogeneity; \citet{fong2021machine} analyze error propagation when ML predictions serve as regression covariates but do not address the effect modifier setting.
In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.

\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups.
This subgroup-varying error is the failure mode we address: it distorts the very contrasts that define the research question, and prior work documents the pattern without providing a correction mechanism for downstream causal estimands.

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
Applied per-subgroup, DSL operates at the estimand level without cross-subgroup borrowing, yielding strictly higher variance than EC-HTE's measurement-model approach (confusion matrix inversion with hierarchical shrinkage).

None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification, requiring instrumental variables or partial identification; our problem is structurally distinct because the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting exact correction through confusion matrices rather than bounds.
Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
Our validation strategy---synthetic DGPs, a semi-synthetic experiment, and real LLM confusion matrices---is consistent with the evaluation methodology in PPI and DSL, which similarly rely on synthetic and semi-synthetic settings where ground-truth quantities are known by construction; Section~\ref{sec:multilm_opensource} supplements this with confusion matrices from four open-source LLMs, confirming that $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity arises in practice.

\section{Comparison with PPI Correction}
\label{app:ppi_comparison}

PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi} constructs confidence intervals by combining a large set of ML predictions with a smaller set of gold-standard labels, using the gold labels to debias the ML-based estimator.
Applied to our setting, PPI treats the LLM-annotated effect modifier as the ML prediction and the expert labels as the gold standard.
Two variants arise naturally: \emph{PPI-global} pools all expert labels to estimate a single rectifier (analogous to our Global baseline), and \emph{PPI-subgroup} estimates per-subgroup rectifiers (analogous to Stratified MLE).
The key difference from confusion-matrix inversion is that PPI does not invert the confusion matrix; instead, it uses the gold labels to directly debias the estimand.
This avoids the matrix inversion step that can amplify noise at small $n_{\text{expert}}$, but it also means PPI cannot exploit the structure of the misclassification process to reduce bias as aggressively.

Table~\ref{tab:ppi_comparison} compares PPI-global, PPI-subgroup, and EC-HTE under the synthetic DGP with $K{=}2$ subgroups and extreme misclassification heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi = 0.20$, $\Delta\tau = 0.5$).
PPI-subgroup achieves stable coverage ($\geq 0.97$) even at $n_{\text{expert}} = 100$, reflecting its conservative variance estimation, but its bias reduction is limited: $|\text{bias}|$ remains at 0.04--0.05 across all budgets because PPI does not perform confusion-matrix inversion.
EC-HTE achieves lower $|\text{bias}|$ at all budgets and lower RMSE at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, where the variance cost of per-subgroup confusion-matrix estimation is offset by its bias reduction.
PPI-global inherits the same bias amplification as Global correction (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), confirming that the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ mechanism operates regardless of the inference framework.

原文："Applied per-subgroup, DSL operates at the estimand level without cross-subgroup borrowing, yielding strictly higher variance..."

\section{Comparison with PPI Correction}
\label{app:ppi_comparison}

PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi} constructs confidence intervals by combining a large set of ML predictions with a smaller set of gold-standard labels, using the gold labels to debias the ML-based estimator.
Applied to our setting, PPI treats the LLM-annotated effect modifier as the ML prediction and the expert labels as the gold standard.
Two variants arise naturally: \emph{PPI-global} pools all expert labels to estimate a single rectifier (analogous to our Global baseline), and \emph{PPI-subgroup} estimates per-subgroup rectifiers (analogous to Stratified MLE).
The key difference from confusion-matrix inversion is that PPI does not invert the confusion matrix; instead, it uses the gold labels to directly debias the estimand.
This avoids the matrix inversion step that can amplify noise at small $n_{\text{expert}}$, but it also means PPI cannot exploit the structure of the misclassification process to reduce bias as aggressively.

Table~\ref{tab:ppi_comparison} compares PPI-global, PPI-subgroup, and EC-HTE under the synthetic DGP with $K{=}2$ subgroups and extreme misclassification heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi = 0.20$, $\Delta\tau = 0.5$).
PPI-subgroup achieves stable coverage ($\geq 0.97$) even at $n_{\text{expert}} = 100$, reflecting its conservative variance estimation, but its bias reduction is limited: $|\text{bias}|$ remains at 0.04--0.05 across all budgets because PPI does not perform confusion-matrix inversion.
EC-HTE achieves lower $|\text{bias}|$ at all budgets and lower RMSE at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, where the variance cost of per-subgroup confusion-matrix estimation is offset by its bias reduction.
PPI-global inherits the same bias amplification as Global correction (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), confirming that the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ mechanism operates regardless of the inference framework.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Measurement error and annotation models.}
Classical measurement error theory shows that correction via estimated error models can amplify MSE when the error structure is misspecified~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}; Bayesian approaches require informative priors when identification is weak~\cite{gustafson2003measurement}, and nonparametric methods use repeated measurements or instruments to recover the true distribution~\cite{hu2008nonparametric}.
We formalize this principle for a specific causal estimand: Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} gives an exact identity for CATE bias under global correction with heterogeneous misclassification.
\citet{ogburn2012nondifferential} show nondifferential confounder misclassification attenuates effects; our setting differs---the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier, and correction can amplify bias.
\citet{battistin2014treatment} study treatment effect estimation with covariate measurement error but focus on average effects rather than subgroup-level heterogeneity; \citet{fong2021machine} analyze error propagation when ML predictions serve as regression covariates but do not address the effect modifier setting.
In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.

\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups.
This subgroup-varying error is the failure mode we address: it distorts the very contrasts that define the research question, and prior work documents the pattern without providing a correction mechanism for downstream causal estimands.

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification, requiring instrumental variables or partial identification; our problem is structurally distinct because the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting exact correction through confusion matrices rather than bounds.
Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
Our validation strategy---synthetic DGPs, a semi-synthetic experiment, and real LLM confusion matrices---is consistent with the evaluation methodology in PPI and DSL, which similarly rely on synthetic and semi-synthetic settings where ground-truth quantities are known by construction; Section~\ref{sec:multilm_opensource} supplements this with confusion matrices from four open-source LLMs, confirming that $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity arises in practice.

19	\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
20	PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
21	In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
22	EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
23	\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
24	None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
25	\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification, requiring instrumental variables or partial identification; our problem is structurally distinct because the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting exact correction through confusion matrices rather than bounds.
26	Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
27	Our validation strategy---synthetic DGPs, a semi-synthetic experiment, and real LLM confusion matrices---is consistent with the evaluation methodology in PPI and DSL, which similarly rely on synthetic and semi-synthetic settings where ground-truth quantities are known by construction; Section~\ref{sec:multilm_opensource} supplements this with confusion matrices from four open-source LLMs, confirming that $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity arises in practice.

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification, requiring instrumental variables or partial identification; our problem is structurally distinct because the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting exact correction through confusion matrices rather than bounds.
Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
Our validation strategy---synthetic DGPs, a semi-synthetic experiment, and real LLM confusion matrices---is consistent with the evaluation methodology in PPI and DSL, which similarly rely on synthetic and semi-synthetic settings where ground-truth quantities are known by construction; Section~\ref{sec:multilm_opensource} supplements this with confusion matrices from four open-source LLMs, confirming that $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity arises in practice.
